OTA commissions run 15–30%. Here’s what hospitality operators actually need from their tech partners. RaftLabs 7 min read · Oct 11, 2026 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Photo by appshunter.io on Unsplash Sixty percent of hotel bookings happen on mobile devices. Your customers expect to book, check in, and unlock their room from their phone. If you’re not offering that, you’re pushing them back to Expedia and Airbnb. And you’re paying 15–30% commission on every booking they make through those platforms. A developer building a hospitality tech product or a founder evaluating mobile apps for your hotel brand faces a straightforward decision: own the guest relationship or rent access to it. Mobile apps are infrastructure, not a feature. And building them right requires understanding both the business case and the technical constraints that most platforms ignore. The commission problem is not actually about commissions Here’s what most hoteliers don’t measure. A guest books through Expedia. The hotel pays 20% commission. But that’s not the real cost. The guest’s email, booking history, preferences, and repeat purchase intent live on Expedia’s servers. Next time the guest travels, they go back to Expedia because that’s where their travel history is. The hotel pays commission again. And again. The guest never becomes a direct customer. OTA commissions compound across customer lifetime value. A guest worth $10,000 in repeat stays over five years costs the hotel $2,000-$3,000 in commissions if those bookings always go through an OTA. A mobile app changes the economics. The guest books once through your app. You own their contact information, preferences, and booking history. Their next stay is frictionless. No commission. Just repeat revenue. For a property doing $100,000/month in bookings, shifting just 20% to a direct app channel saves $30,000-$60,000 annually in commissions. Multiply that across a portfolio and the number becomes substantial. Why mobile websites fail You might have a mobile-responsive website. Guests can search your property and see room types. But try booking a hotel room on a mobile website. You’re filling out forms on a small screen, typing payment information with your thumbs, dealing with slow page loads. The experience is friction. Now try the same booking through a well-designed mobile app. Your payment information is saved. The interface is fast. You complete the booking in seconds. The difference in conversion matters. Apps convert mobile traffic at higher rates because the experience is optimized for actual use rather than adapted from desktop. Guests complete bookings they would have abandoned on a website. That’s not just about user experience. That’s revenue. The real operational problem apps solve Mobile apps solve a problem that hotel operations teams live with every day: peak check-in. A bus full of guests arrives. The front desk has three people. Guest lines stretch across the lobby. Service suffers. Staff gets frustrated. Guests get frustrated. Mobile check-in with digital keys eliminates this entirely. Guests check in on their phone before they arrive. They receive their room assignment and digital key. They walk straight to their room. The front desk handles guests who actually need help. That operational efficiency becomes more important as labor costs rise and finding hospitality staff gets harder. Technology that moves routine transactions away from human staff frees your team to deliver actual hospitality instead of processing paperwork. White-label platforms versus custom development Your first question: should we build or buy? White-label platforms offer pre-built apps you brand with your colors and property details. The vendor handles infrastructure, app store submissions, and ongoing maintenance. Pricing is typically low upfront, then monthly fees per property. The trade-offs become clear quickly. You’re limited to whatever features the platform offers. Your app looks similar to hundreds of other properties on the same platform. Your guest data lives in their servers. And if you want to switch platforms later, migrating that data is expensive or impossible. For one or two properties, white-label makes sense while you validate whether apps actually drive bookings. But at five properties or beyond, the economics shift. Custom development costs more upfront but scales differently. Adding a sixth property to a custom platform costs configuration and training. Adding a sixth property to a white-label platform costs another monthly subscription. Over three years, a portfolio operator with five properties paying $100–200/month per property in white-label fees pays $18,000-$36,000 just in licensing. A custom platform built for $40,000-$60,000 pays back in 12–18 months and then costs only maintenance. Custom development also means you own the code and the data. You control what integrations exist. You can differentiate with features unique to your brand. You’re not competing on the same platform as everyone else.
